💡 Key Takeaways
  • Homo erectus might have also lived in rainforests — previously thought to be a habitat in which only modern humans could have thrived.Credit: S.
  • According to recent reports, fossil teeth suggest that Homo erectus thrived in dense rainforests in southern China as recently as 180,000 years ago.
  • Artificial-intelligence giant Anthropic has made history with the largest initial public offering (IPO) on record on 19 November.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Homo erectus might have also lived in rainforests — previously thought to be a habitat in which only modern humans could have thrived.Credit: S. Entressangle/E. Daynes/SPL.

According to recent reports, fossil teeth suggest that Homo erectus thrived in dense rainforests in southern China as recently as 180,000 years ago. Researchers had thought that these ancient hominins had been limited to savannahs and open woodlands, says Kira Westaway, a geochronologist and a co-author of two upcoming studies. “This is a really major deal, because we thought Homo sapiens were the only species that had the skill set to survive in really challenging rainforest environments.”.

Reference: Nature paper 1 & paper 2.

Artificial-intelligence giant Anthropic has made history with the largest initial public offering (IPO) on record on 19 November. The firm — now valued at a staggering US$1.5 trillion — has major ambitions in science. It made waves earlier this year when it reported that its model Claude had made several major mathematics breakthroughs. The company also debuted their first ‘wet’ laboratory for life sciences research and has announced looks to “substantially” scale up its work in AI-enabled drug discovery. Pitched as a company that prioritizes AI safety, some researchers question whether an IPO — and the accompanying investor demands — might disrupt some of Anthropic’s safety commitments.

It has been revealed that roughly 180 million people could be carrying a previously unknown type of giant virus in their guts. Researchers found DNA from these ‘egoviruses’ in gut samples from people, buffalo, goats, chickens, deer and pigs. Six clades were unique to people, one of which is estimated to be present in roughly 1% of the population. Microbiologists say that egoviruses could be the missing link between giant viruses that infect single-celled organisms and distantly related poxviruses, such as those that cause smallpox and mpox, which can infect people and animals directly.

Here in Washington DC, tens of thousands of researchers have gathered for the Society for Neuroscience’s annual meeting — a showcase for everything from neural implants to memory research.

According to recent reports, but when I asked a panel of leaders at the US National Institutes of Health what in neuroscience remains underappreciated, several pointed to the brain’s relationship with the rest of the body. Nora Volkow, director of the National Institute on Drug Abuse, lamented the lack of research into brain metabolism — a blind spot exposed by the surprising neurological effects of GLP-1 drugs.

Industry observers note that amy Bany Adams, acting director of the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke, offered a reminder of how much remains to be discovered. Of the glymphatic system, the brain’s waste-clearance network, she noted: “We didn’t even know it existed when I was in graduate school.” I’m leaving with a longer list of questions about what else we’ve been overlooking.

Industry observers note that neuroscientists are uncovering how the brain orchestrates a tailored mixture of symptoms in response to either a bacterial or viral infection. Presenting at the Society for Neuroscience’s annual meeting on 15 November, researchers suggested that the brain decodes the type of pathogen that has invaded, accesses memories of past bouts of illness and can even mobilize immune defences at the sight of a sick person. The unpublished findings challenge the long-held view that neurological responses to infection are a one-size-fits-all response to inflammation.

It has been revealed that artificial-intelligence governance requires more than companies’ oversight of their models — it requires “a system of accountability” that works like a national constitution, argues legal scholar Cindy Skach. Firms should be held legally liable when individuals are affected by AI actions that infringe on their fundamental rights, Skach suggests. She proposes ‘human dignity’ as the most important value for the system to uphold. When a person’s dignity is violated — by an AI-generated deepfake or by a chatbot that treats a distressed user as just another interaction — they could petition a court directly to hold the perpetrator accountable.

Do you find networking a nightmare? Three experts share — in the form of short videos — how to grasp the nettle. They suggest thinking about networking as a professional skill that can be learnt and developed, considering arriving early for events and not worrying about volume. One high-quality connection and follow-up conversation is worth more than 100 business cards, says public-speaking coach Susie Ashfield.

In the second episode of Nature Podcast’s climate miniseries, host Nick Petrić Howe hears from scientists about what humanity can actually do to stop the runaway train of rising temperatures. The rise of renewable-energy technologies is already making a dent in greenhouse-gas emissions, experts say. But creating meat alternatives and a move away from an economic system that incentivizes ‘growth at any cost’ could help to really shift the dial.

Nature Podcast | 45 min listen or read the transcript.

Sources indicate that vertebrate palaeontologist Aldo Benites-Palomino explains why the extinct ancient whale — which evolved extreme facial asymmetry to to make space in its head for echolocation and sound production organs — was named with a Peruvian word for “anything that is flashy, over-the-top, bizarre, extravagant or difficult to categorize aesthetically”. (Discover | 7 min read).

Reference: Communications Biology paper.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03797-3.

According to recent reports, today I’m considering buying a prickly pear cactus (Opuntia) in case of a power cut. Researchers have found that the plants’ unusual method of photosynthesis can be harnessed to generate a small amount of electricity, with around eight prickly pears together generating nearly three times the voltage of a standard AA battery.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Published: 15:32 EST, 22 November 2026 | Updated: 15:36 EST, 22 November 2026.

Just when they thought they were beginning to make some progress, along comes another embarrassing setback for Hibs and the decision-makers who have led them into this most trying of seasons.

Before the international break, the impression was that their recently-appointed head coach Marink Reedijk had turned a corner with that Premier Sports Cup semi-final victory over Hearts at Hampden and a 4-0 win at Pittodrie.

Well, if he did, it has taken them headlong into another cul-de-sac. That’s how it felt at Easter Road yesterday when they were trounced 4-0 by Dundee United and left second-bottom of the Premiership table with more than a third of the season completed.

It made rather a mockery of the club’s social media channels, the profile pages of which proudly trumpet their newfound status as ‘Premier Sports Cup finalists’… with an exclamation mark and a golden trophy emoji thrown in for good measure.

In a recent development, self-respecting Hibs fans won’t be fooled by the propaganda. Not after a humiliating afternoon on which their much-vaunted anthem, ’Sunshine on Leith’, was belted out by a gleeful away support at Easter Road.

Long before Zac Sapsford’s first-half double and strikes after the interval by Lyall Cameron and Jesse Randall, some supporters were digging out their anti-board banners and using a megaphone to voice their frustration with those upstairs.

Malky Mackay is under growing pressure from supporters in his role as Hibs sporting director.

Zac Sapsford scores the first of Dundee United 's four goals against Hibs at Easter Road.

Dundee boss Steven Pressley claims that he alone was to blame for their 8-0 thrashing by Hearts.

This is how it works at struggling clubs, where fans need someone to blame. First, they target players. Then they single out the manager. When his replacement proves to be no more effective, they have little option but to turn their guns on the board.

Recent findings suggest that not that there’s anything wrong with holding the hierarchy to account if they are the common denominator in a lengthy period of under-achievement. There has been little sign of progress at Easter Road since Bournemouth owner Bill Foley sold his Hibs shares back to the Gordon family last year, having suggested that they didn’t listen to his input. Substantial questions are also being asked of sporting director Malky Mackay who was asked in 2024 to lead and oversee the entire football operation, including recruitment and the appointment of a head coach.

Recent findings suggest that club legend David Gray had his moments as manager, but in the end, supporters wanted rid. Reedijk may turn out to be the real deal but the early signs are that he is struggling with the squad he has inherited. Too many of them failed to do the basics yesterday.

Unlike Hibs, Jim Goodwin’s Dundee United are a strong side with a clear identity. Not for nothing have they gone eight games without defeat, but they scored all too easily as they racked up their biggest-ever victory at Easter Road.

In a recent development, hibs’ squad appears to be weak, imbalanced and too full of ill-advised signings for Reedijk to make the kind of impact he would like. The holes in it are such that he recently opted to use Scotland defender Grant Hanley as an emergency centre-forward.

Reedijk needs to begin an overhaul of that playing staff in the January window, but how much power will be granted in that process? The Dutch coach has already hinted that he will not be given the final say when it comes to transfers.

According to recent reports, the fans are nervous about another rebuild under Mackay and his recruitment staff, whose work in the summer window left a lot to be desired. Jason Kerr was a double-winner with St Johnstone, but he has cut a hapless figure at the back. Midfielder Azeem Abdulai, signed on a three-year contract from Leyton Orient, has made only four appearances, just one from the start. And then there is striker Nathan Lowe, on loan from Stoke City, who is struggling to adapt.

Mackay’s record is under heavy scrutiny. He is to be commended for making a profit of around £6million on striker Kieron Bowie, but why has there been no substantial replacement since the striker’s move to Italy nearly a year ago? Can he really argue that expensive signings such as Thibault Klidje and Ante Suto have been value for money?

A club of Hibs’ size, with those resources, should not be in the relegation zone. Nor should they be struggling so pitifully in their own stadium – they have lost nine of their last ten league games there and haven’t taken three points at home since April.

Which tees up nicely Dundee’s visit to Easter Road on Tuesday, not least because the Tayside club suffered a humiliation of their own this weekend. While Hibs were conceding four, Steven Pressley's side were shipping eight in a hammering by Hearts that has surely inflicted significant psychological damage.

In a recent development, to his great credit, Pressley insisted afterwards that he alone was to blame for his team’s wretched performance. That may have been true on the night, but over an extended period, a club’s fortunes tend to be shaped by decisions off the pitch. As Hibs have been finding out.

Will Australia push for fossil fuel exit at UN talks?

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • "Renewable energy, grids, storage and electrification are creating opportunities to strengthen resilience, improve energy security, and reduce emissions at the same time," said Chris Bowen, Australia's climate change and energy minister, in October during a meeting in Fiji ahead of the COP climate conference.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In its role as president of negotiations at the UN climate talks in Turkey, Australia is being pressured to guide nations toward unified action on slashing the greenhouse gas emissions that are generated in large part by burning fossil fuels.

The nation has pledged to lead by example at the summit through a strong commitment to renewable energy, electrification and reduced reliance on planet-heating coal, oil and gas.

"Renewable energy, grids, storage and electrification are creating opportunities to strengthen resilience, improve energy security, and reduce emissions at the same time," said Chris Bowen, Australia's climate change and energy minister, in October during a meeting in Fiji ahead of the COP climate conference.

"These are proven, commercial and scalable today. Now is the moment for faster implementation.".

Recent findings suggest that yet Australia is also the world's third-largest exporter of fossil fuels. And unlike France and Germany, or island nations from Fiji to the Bahamas that are highly vulnerable to a changing climate, the COP31 co-president has not yet committed to phasing them out.

As calls grow for the country to set a clear route to a clean energy future, critics say its vague promise to transition away from polluting sources of power does not go far enough.

Australia is home to 56% of the world's coal mine projects currently in the pipeline, notes environmental nonprofit, 350.org.

Andreas Sieber, head of political strategy at the organization, is calling on the country, the world's second-largest coal exporter, to reverse course and announce an "overdue coal phaseout date" during the COP31 conference.

"Australia needs to walk the walk and follow Germany's example and commit to a phaseout," said Melanie Pill, founder of The Climate Project, an Australia-based climate policy advisory.

The argument to end fossil fuel production is not only about cutting emissions but reducing dependence on energy systems that rely on volatile oil and gas markets, she explained.

"A fossil phaseout in the face of the enduring and escalating conflict in the Middle East is in the interest of everyone," Pill told DW.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

This is especially true for Australia's diesel-reliant Pacific neighbors, who spend up to 25% of GDP on fossil fuel imports — as opposed 6% on health — according to a report by the Institute for Climate Risk and Response at the University of Newly introduced South Wales.

As lead negotiator at the UN climate talks, Australia can "flip the narrative" on a fossil fuel phaseout, using the challenge of energy security as a justification, stated Pill.

This opportunity could be lost, however, if Australia fails to address fossil fuel exports that accounted for 80% of its total carbon footprint in 2022 — and near 5% of global emissions.

While the nation is a world leader in rooftop solar, and generates around half of its electricity from renewables, this progress is "being undone by its continued approval of more fossil fuels for export," said Simon Bradshaw, COP31 lead and climate expert at Greenpeace Australia Pacific.

He noted that the Labor government of Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has approved the construction, expansion or extension of 38 coal, oil and gas projects since coming to power four years ago on a pro-climate platform.

"You cannot aspire to lead on climate abroad if you're not getting your own house in order," stated Thomas Houlie, climate and energy policy analyst at Climate Analytics, a global climate policy institute.

In 2025, when Australia approved the extension of a major gas export project in the country's west until 2070, Albanese justified the move in the name of a balance between "security of energy supply" and "support [for] the transition which reduces our emissions.".

It has been revealed that the country has publicly backed a global transition away from the fossil fuels driving the global temperature rise linked to extreme heat and drought. Both through the Global Stocktake agreed at the 2023 UN climate summit, and via the inaugural "transitioning away" summit in Colombia this April, at which Australia and 56 countries pledged to develop a fossil fuel exit road map.

But these commitments are not reflected in Australian resources policy, or its domestic rollout of clean power infrastructure.

"While the government has set a renewables target for electricity, it leaves plenty of blind spots in other sectors," noted Houlie, adding that emission reductions in industry and transport have been limited and that the push to achieve an 82% renewables target for the electricity grid by 2030 is behind schedule.

In its role as lead negotiator at COP31, Australia has promised to ensure that any final conference text serves to "elevate the views and the experiences" of small Pacific nations in its region, from Vanuatu to Tuvalu.

These island countries that generate low emissions yet suffer extreme climate impacts from worsening cyclones or rising seas are "sick of Australia's double talk on climate," said Shiva Gounden, head of Pacific at Greenpeace Australia Pacific.

Australia must commit to "substantial newly introduced funding contributions" to help Pacific neighbors adapt to the climate emergency and achieve energy independence, said his colleague Bradshaw. He reiterated the need to concurrently create a "national road map" away from coal and gas production and export.

According to recent reports, A Climate Analytics report co-authored by Houlie outlines a fossil fuel phaseout pathway for Australia that can begin immediately. This includes an end to coal power generation by 2034 and a rapid reduction in oil and gas consumption, with renewables generating almost all the country's electricity by 2040. Fossil fuel export projects would be eliminated, and existing ones shuttered before becoming obsolete.

"This co-presidency is a golden opportunity for Australia to step up and commit to a phaseout," remarked Houlie.

When Manchester City play like this what a loss their football will be to the Premier League – and the Champions League – if they are heavily sanctioned later this season.

It has been revealed that in what turned out to be a match for the ages, a night of brilliant, unbridled attack, we were treated to the ultimate game of two halves as the back-to-back European champions Paris St-Germain took City apart for 45 minutes. And then were left holding on.

According to recent reports, city will hope this is a sign of what is to come in their Premier League fight. But with a different result. After suffering a resounding defeat at the hands of the Premier League’s independent commission, with 114 of the 115 charges against them proven, they maintain their innocence and are mounting an appeal.

It has been revealed that could they make a comeback? It would be incredible and highly improbable if they did so but, out on the pitch, and 3-0 down after a first half in which they were in danger of being humiliated by PSG, they created enough opportunities to save themselves.

The data backed that. City’s expected goals (xG) was 2.57 while PSG’s was 1.83. City had 27 shots to 15 and had more possession and more passes. Enzo Maresca made a triple substitution to devastating effect, especially with the introduction of fresh signings Ayyoub Bouaddi and Iliman Ndiaye.

In the end they clawed back two goals, both scored by Erling Haaland, who now has 61 in 60 games in this competition – seventh outright in the all-time list, before Ruud van Nistelrooy. And 37 of those for City, overtaking Sergio Agüero’s club record.

“Even with 3-0 in the first half, with the amount of chances we created in the second half, we deserved more. Luis [Enrique, PSG’s coach] remarked at the end of the game that they were quite lucky,” Maresca claimed before being asked whether he would relish facing PSG again, later in this competition. “My feeling is we are there. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Published: 18:00 EST, 22 November 2026 | Updated: 18:11 EST, 22 November 2026.

Let’s face it, Neil McCann was never the most popular of appointments with Kilmarnock fans, but not even his harshest critics could deny that he did a fine job in keeping the club in Scotland’s top flight last season.

Unfortunately for him, it looks increasingly likely that he isn’t going to get the chance to repeat the trick this time around.

According to recent reports, the writing already appears to be on the wall for the 52-year-old. A question of when, rather than if, he is given his jotters.

According to recent reports, by all accounts, he hasn’t lost the dressing room. Which is just as well, because he has well and truly lost the punters, whose collective mood shifted from angry to apathetic over the course of 90-odd thoroughly entertaining minutes at Rugby Park on Saturday.

When that happens, it’s a long way back.

McCann knows this himself. It is not as if he is operating with the blinkers on.

It's a tough watch for Neil McCann as his Kilmarnock team go down 4-2 to Aberdeen.

His assessment of his team’s performances week-to-week tends to be pretty honest, as it was again this weekend.

The problem is, as he put it, that he is coming across ‘like a broken record’.

It has been revealed that his team are hopeless at the back and toothless up top, with some encouraging stuff in between. If the supporters are sick of hearing it, imagine how scunnered McCann must feel saying it. He certainly looks it.

If they continue to defend like this, relegation is a nailed-on certainty.

Recent findings suggest that they shipped four here — and it could have very easily been a few more — to take their tally to 33 conceded for the season in just 14 games. It’s laughable, there’s no other way to dress it up.

Aberdeen’s Kevin Nisbet scored twice in four first-half minutes, capitalising on a woeful clearance from keeper Nico Mantl to put the Dons ahead, before curling a free-kick straight through the weakest wall you’ve ever seen in your life to double the visitors’ advantage.

New Dons boss Mario Frick can't hide his delight after victory in first game in charge.

Sources indicate that the third goal — shortly after Greg Kiltie had given McCann’s men a lifeline — was the worst of the lot. Former Rugby Park skipper Brad Lyons ghosted in behind the completely unaware Michael Schjonning-Larsen to head the ball home after Cathal McCarthy failed to stop Nesta Guinness-Walker’s cross from the left touchline.

Shocking stuff all round, and exactly the type of goal which has killed Killie all season — and will continue to do so until something drastic changes.

Let’s not forget, the recent international break afforded McCann and his staff a fortnight to work on things on the training pitch ahead of what is going to be a gruelling winter schedule.

In a recent development, while the Killie manager will ultimately be the one to pay the price, his players need to have a right good look at themselves too. There was simply no sign of anyone in that backline taking any sort of responsibility.

Kilmarnock’s next three games are against St Mirren, Hibernian and Motherwell — the three sides presently directly above them in the table.

An absolute minimum of four points from that run is required, otherwise this is going to get rather ugly. In truth, defeat in Paisley this weekend may well be the final nail in McCann’s coffin.

On the other hand, things are finally starting to look up for the Dons.

New manager Mario Frick has promised to bring heavy metal football to these shores, and if Saturday is anything to go by, the ex-Liechtenstein international is a man of his word.

McCann's job looks to be on the line after bottom club Killie succumbed to another defeat.

His team were a joy to watch going forward here, particularly in the first half.

It was a million miles away from the kind of turgid football offered up under his predecessor as Dons manager, Stephen Robinson.

Speed, intensity, aggression, quality. The performance was full of it.

You could count the number of times the Dons faffed about with the ball on one hand. Every time there was an opportunity to get forward, they took it.

Ante Palaversa, making his first appearance of the campaign, was at the heart of it.

Industry observers note that for whatever reason, Robinson never fancied the Croatian, a stance which perplexed the Pittodrie faithful. Indeed, the 26-year-old — once on the books of Manchester City — was deemed surplus to requirements over the summer.

The Dons will be delighted there were no takers.

It has been revealed that he was outstanding here as he commanded that space between midfield and defence without breaking sweat. Nobody in Killie colours could get near him.

Both Nicky Devlin and Guinness-Walker bombed up their respective wings all day, while some of the link-up play between Nisbet — who should have had a hat-trick before Findlay Marshall wrapped things up late on — and Hicham Mahou was delightful.

Defensively, they were all over the shop at times, and no doubt they will be punished heavily at Ibrox on Tuesday night if they are as open as this.

Industry observers note that but this was a display to simply be enjoyed rather than picked apart. It makes a change.

#140240. Why electrification is the climate game changer we need

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dw ↗ Open Full Page

Why electrification is the climate game changer we need

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (674 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Electrification isn't just a buzzword, it's a lever that could slash energy bills while reducing the world's dependency on coal, oil and gas.
  • If fuel-importing countries "speed up the electrification of their economies considerably" they could knock more than $400 billion (€357 billion) off their energy import bills by 2035 compared with 2025 levels.
  • In a nutshell, electrification means replacing technologies that burn fossil fuels such as oil and gas with electric alternatives.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Electrification isn't just a buzzword, it's a lever that could slash energy bills while reducing the world's dependency on coal, oil and gas. Which also means significantly slashing the heat-trapping CO2 emissions that are linked to flooding and extreme heat around the world.

If fuel-importing countries "speed up the electrification of their economies considerably" they could knock more than $400 billion (€357 billion) off their energy import bills by 2035 compared with 2025 levels. That is according to a recent analysis by the International Energy Agency, which also found that such an acceleration could mean the world needs 18 million fewer barrels of oil per day.

In a nutshell, electrification means replacing technologies that burn fossil fuels such as oil and gas with electric alternatives. That means switching from diesel cars to electric vehicles (EVs), turning off gas heating and using electricity to power heat pumps.

In a recent development, but the way the electricity running these things is generated is also key. In theory, an EV using power created in a coal-heavy electricity grid could be worse for the climate than a car running on gas.

Electricity derived from renewable energy sources such as solar, wind or hydropower on the other hand produces clean power.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

In a recent development, the booming EV market is the fastest-growing electrification sector. Globally, one in four cars sold in 2025 was electric and since 2020, international sales have increased by almost 600%.

Nonetheless, electricity only covers about 20% of final energy use in the wider global economy, including that used in businesses, factories and people's homes.

It would need to supply more than half of all power by 2050 if we are to avoid runaway heating and the more intense and extreme weather events connected to a hotter climate.

Some industries and activities are harder to electrify than others. While it's relatively easy to switch to EVs and decarbonize buildings, some industries such as petrochemicals and steel use fossil fuels as raw materials to make products like plastics, fertilizer, detergent or steel.

In addition, while heat pumps work well for low-temperature needs, they can't replace the temperatures needed in steelmaking or cement production.

The World Resources Institute, an independent research organization, recommends hydrogen, synthetic fuels or other low-carbon alternatives as more viable options than electrification in cases such as ocean shipping and aviation.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

In addition to cutting down on greenhouse gas emissions resulting in cleaner air and limiting global heating, electrification is also more efficient and cheaper in the long run.

A combustion engine in a car wastes as much as 80% of its fuel energy, mostly to turn it into heat. Only about 20% is converted to actually move the car. Electric motors, on the other hand, convert about 80% of electrical energy into motion.

It has been revealed that as the World Resources Institute points out, running all appliances on electricity will increase electricity consumption. Yet total energy costs are likely to be lower, even if electricity becomes more expensive.

As electricity needs grow due to the rapid expansion of AI, data centers and the overall shift to a more electrified world, outpaced grids struggle to keep up. This is increasingly holding back the energy transition, delaying the rollout of additional renewable generation, storage capacity and electrified demand.

According to the International Energy Agency, annual grid investment has to increase by about 50% by 2030 from today's $400 billion.

There's also a major mismatch between how long it takes to set up newly introduced grid infrastructure (five to 15 years), compared to renewable energy projects (one to five years), and EV charging infrastructure (one to two years).

Experts say we need smarter grids that support a two-way flow of electricity while remaining secure, stable and able to keep up with higher demand as electrification intensifies.

  • Corentin Tolisso opened the scoring for the hosts and Ernest Nuamah doubled Lyon’s advantage late in a first half devoid of any shots on target for the visitors.
  • Yéremy Pino halved the deficit five minutes after the break, before Pavel Sulc restored the two-goal lead, and substitute Daichi Kamada’s late goal proved a mere consolation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Pierre Sage felt Crystal Palace were “really far off” his expectations after suffering a 3-2 away Europa League defeat by his former side Lyon.

Corentin Tolisso opened the scoring for the hosts and Ernest Nuamah doubled Lyon’s advantage late in a first half devoid of any shots on target for the visitors.

Yéremy Pino halved the deficit five minutes after the break, before Pavel Sulc restored the two-goal lead, and substitute Daichi Kamada’s late goal proved a mere consolation.

“At the end, we were frustrated by the result, but in the first half we have to be frustrated in the way we play,” noted Sage, speaking to PalaceTV.

“I think we didn’t play this first half. We are really far off our standards in the mental side of the play, in the tactical side of the play, because the players are too high between our lines and we really struggled a lot with that.

“When you give back the ball to your opponent, you suffer a lot and we were better in the second half. You cannot win this kind of game by playing only one half.”.

Sage’s side got the better of his predecessor, Oliver Glasner, after they bounced back to beat Nottingham Forest 3-1 at Selhurst Park on Sunday.

After that victory, the Frenchman called for more consistency from his team, but on Thursday night was left ruing missed opportunities and goals conceded too easily by last season’s Conference League winners.

Sources indicate that sage was sacked by Lyon in January 2025 after a 14-month spell with the Ligue 1 outfit. Like Glasner’s, his own reunion ended in disappointment.

In a recent development, he told Uefa: “It’s a very disappointing return because we lost. I can’t take satisfaction from coming back home or seeing familiar faces when the result isn’t there.

“The scoreline may have been close, but there was a significant difference in the way the two teams played.

“We improved considerably after the break and gave ourselves a chance, but conceding that third goal made things difficult.

“I think our second-half efforts deserved an equaliser, although winning would have been a generous reward given that we only really played [to our level] for one half.”.

Recent findings suggest that the veteran captain said: “It has been a long time coming. The fans were up for it, the players were up for it so we’re very happy with the performance.”.

When asked about Evanilson’s header, which Smith supplied the assist for, he replied: “It wasn’t my best cross but I put it in an area, what a finish from him and I think we deserved that little bit of luck.

“From there on we went on to win the game but in the second half we got a little bit tired but the quality that came off the bench is great and we look forward to Sunday now.

“It’s a great header, he deserved it because he has worked very hard this season and many more to come from him.”.

#140238. Tech Report: Borussia Dortmund's Felix Nmecha and the question of religion

Tech Report: Borussia Dortmund's Felix Nmecha and the question of religion

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (842 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Felix Nmecha's renewed use of the "Crowns down celebration" — where a crown is pretended to be removed from someone's head and placed at Jesus' feet — has sparked a reaction from Borussia Dortmund's official supporters' group.
  • Borussia Dortmund is a club for everyone," read a statement after the Bundesliga club beat Elversberg, a game in which Nmecha scored twice.
  • "In the past, the the Borussia Dortmund supporters club has deliberately refrained from commenting on sports-related issues and the athletic performance of individual players.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Felix Nmecha's renewed use of the "Crowns down celebration" — where a crown is pretended to be removed from someone's head and placed at Jesus' feet — has sparked a reaction from Borussia Dortmund's official supporters' group.

"Faith does not justify exclusion. Faith does not justify division. Borussia Dortmund is a club for everyone," read a statement after the Bundesliga club beat Elversberg, a game in which Nmecha scored twice. Nmecha's first documented "Crowns down celebration" was at the 2026 World Cup, for which "The King's Return" campaign was launched.

"In the past, the the Borussia Dortmund supporters club has deliberately refrained from commenting on sports-related issues and the athletic performance of individual players. We remain committed to this approach," the statement continued.

"However, when it comes to our club's values, discrimination, and the question of what view of humanity is fostered within and around Borussia Dortmund, we cannot and will not remain silent.".

The fan club states their issue is not with Nmecha being a devout Christian, but rather his public support for "The King's Return" campaign, which the supporters club said "gives us cause to reassess the situation.".

This campaign, according to research by German public broadcaster ARD in the summer of 2026, was designed by the "Ballers in God" (MAJOR) network. BIG was founded in 2015 by footballer John Bostock, a devout Christian who wanted to create a community where professional footballers could strengthen each other in their faith, pray together, and read the Bible. In over a decade since, the BIG community has grown to nearly 800,000 followers on Instagram.

Nmecha issued a response on social media not long afterwards, writing:.

"I've been told that my most recent goal celebration has led to some misunderstandings," Nmecha wrote.

"My message was never intended to spread intolerance, discrimination, or hatred in any form. As Christians, our message is one of love and respect for every person—regardless of where someone comes from, what they believe in, or what worldview they hold.".

Reports suggest that both the board at Dortmund and Germany head coach Jürgen Klopp will speak to Nmecha on the matter in the coming days.

Sources indicate that the fan club say their criticism is "directed at religious networks that, under the guise of faith, promote a worldview in which people are devalued or marginalized because of their sexual orientation, gender identity, lifestyle, or personal choices... When religious beliefs are used to deny people their dignity or equality, that is where our tolerance for intolerance ends.".

Industry observers note that here, they are referring to the recent ARD investigation. That work revealed the homepage for "The King's Return" campaign featured a link to a live counseling chat run by US-based evangelical nonprofit Groundwire. During the investigations, counselors told reporters that abortion is "Satan's blueprint" and that homosexuality is a sin.

Borussia Dortmund's statement of core values commits the club to diversity, human rights, and inclusion regardless of gender, sexual orientation, faith, or background. The club's largest and most influential fan group also promotes progressive, anti-fascist, and inclusive values. It is also part of a wider fan landscape in Germany where club members are more involved in club decisions than in many other countries. This was evidenced when the club signed a deal with arms manufacturer Rheinmetall two years ago and in the case of Nmecha as well. When the midfielder signed for Dortmund in 2023, many of the club's fans protested because the player had previously shared or liked several transphobic and homophobic posts on his Instagram account. In response, Nmecha deleted some posts and instead issued a statement emphasizing "I do not discriminate against anyone.".

Article 4 of German Basic Law guarantees that each individual is allowed to decide how strongly, why and which god to believe in. In football, players cannot display political, religious, or personal slogans, statements, or images on their jerseys, undershirts, or gear. However, physical gestures are allowed so long as they don't delay the game or antagonize the crowd.

According to recent reports, the use of physical religious gestures has history in sports, as professor Paul Putz described in his book "The Spirit of the Game: American Christianity and Big-Time Sports". Putz describes how the the pioneers of the Christian athlete movement realized they: "could influence others to Christian ideals more effectively on the field than in the pulpit.".

And yet, such gestures can also be at odds with the atmosphere of modern sports arenas, particularly football. In their book "Sports and Christianity: Historical and Contemporary Perspectives", Nick J. Watson and Andrew Parker explain how modern sport has become a substitute for traditional faith.

"Sport seduces the teeming 'global village'; it is the upcoming opiate of the masses; it is one of the great modern experiences … Sport, for many, has replaced religion as a source of emotional catharsis and spiritual passion," they wrote.

With the 26-year-old Nmecha a key player for both club and country, the conversation around faith and football looks set to continue for some time yet.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, “Captain Underpants”. The laughter that follows is infectious. It seems doubtful that it was an honest answer to the question posed to Zach Lee by the young boy located somewhere near the front of the classroom: “What is your favourite book?” But it got exactly the reaction he was after.

The room is abuzz. It has been for much of the past hour.

Goalkeeper Lee and five of his Everton Under-21s teammates have gleefully taken up the task of being reading buddies to the children of Ellesmere Port’s Meadow Primary School, one of six schools that make up the recently renamed Everton Multi-Academy Trust (EMAT). Seven miles away, six of their Under-21 peers are doing likewise at Oldfield Primary School in Chester.

Nearer to Liverpool, the hollers that greeted Everton Women’s Holly McNamara and Karen Holmgaard 24 hours earlier are still reverberating around the corridors of Bidston Avenue Primary School.

Recent findings suggest that christian Nørgaard and close friends Tyler Dibling and Tyrique George are also familiar with the noise the pupils at the Birkenhead school can make. Last month, the trio were serenaded with a ukulele rendition of Spirit of the Blues on a visit there. Blue ukuleles, of course.

If the colour of the musical instruments is a cute indicator of the strengthening ties between the football club and the EMAT schools, the time being spared by the players is of much greater significance.

In a recent development, it is intended to demonstrate a cross-Club connection with EMAT, which sits alongside Everton in the Community as one of Everton’s associated organisations. “Part of the Everton family,” as Everton’s Chief Tax and Sustainability Officer and Chair of Trustees for EMAT Alison Haynes puts it.

Industry observers note that but there is a deeper intention, too. “We want to use the power of the Everton crest to inspire and engage youngsters in education,” says Steven Baker OBE, CEO of EMAT. Baker has seen this in evidence for more than a decade, having previously served as Principal of Everton Alternative Provision Free School, the award-winning L4 facility that offers youngsters who have struggled in mainstream schools a route back into education.

Sources indicate that lee and his Under-21 colleagues, McNamara and Holmgaard are all supporting one particular mission of EMAT - to inspire youngsters towards a life-long love of reading. More immediately, to ensure they have the requisite literacy level to adequately prepare them for what lies ahead in secondary school education.

According to recent reports, in Ellesmere Port, Chester and Birkenhead, the players are tackling their role head on. Books - donated by Everton staff to help replenish the schools’ libraries - are strewn across the tables and spilling onto the floor. No-one’s troubled by the mess.

It has been revealed that julia Donaldson’s greatest hits are being played out across the room. Michael Morpurgo – a childhood favourite author of midfielder Jack Patterson – can be heard, too. ‘Bluey’ is an appropriately named hit on another table. And then there’s Lee and a group of little ones giggling at Captain Underpants.

Close by to the classroom at Meadow, Everton’s leading post-war goalscorer Graeme Sharp is here too, continuing the literacy theme by officially opening the school’s newly-refurbished library.

In a recent development, “These children will remember today,” claims Baker. “They will remember players from Everton coming into school and taking the time to sit with them.

“They love hearing stories but they also love having someone to read to. Both aspects are so vital for a child’s development.”.

It has been revealed that as is music. It’s why Dibling, George and Norgaard found themselves being taught the chords to one of Goodison’s – and now Hill Dickinson Stadium’s – favourite tunes last month.

Studies show a direct correlation between a child mastering a musical instrument and making their mark in maths and other creative fields.

The Toffees trio left behind gifts of recorders (blue ones), helping the school expand the opportunities it can offer to its pupils.

“We find it’s really vital for their resilience and it's good for the children mentally and socially to have the opportunity to not only play an instrument, but to play to an audience,” says Bidston Avenue headteacher Stuart Brady, a Tranmere Rovers fan.

Recent findings suggest that “It's great for us as a school to have the connection we do with Everton and the players. Days like this are great, but it's also about the children feeling they belong to something bigger.”.

And the proof that EMAT is getting it right is stacking up. In 2024, Everton Free School and Everton Football College – the two original schools on which the Trust was founded – were jointly awarded an ‘Outstanding’ rating by Ofsted. Earlier this year, the respected national TES Awards named EMAT (then The People’s Learning Trust) as its Trust of the Year for trusts with nine schools or fewer.

With the support of a Premier League football club and its players behind them, it is hoped the collective will continue to go from strength to strength.

The intention is that Everton’s Under-21s will return to the schools to resume their reading buddy duties at junctures throughout the season, strengthening their bonds with the schools and pupils. It is seen as a vital part of the players’ professional development.

According to recent reports, representatives from the Men’s and Women’s team will continue to play their part also. Merlin Röhl has already been a guest of Oldfield Primary School’s after-school chess club, taking up an invitation to share his love of the ancient game with the next generation.

According to recent reports, “We understand the responsibility and influence we have as a football club when it comes to our communities,” indicates Haynes. “And you cannot understate the impact the player visits have.

“The atmosphere and the smiles you see in the room, the energy they give to the children… it’s truly wonderful.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The disruption of multiple computer systems run by Microsoft, US air traffic control, the bank JPMorgan Chase and even the US National Security Agency has renewed concerns about the resilience of critical digital infrastructure.
  • At the same time, researchers have reported artificial intelligence -assisted discovery of security flaws in Java and PHP software, while hackers have used AI tools to target supermarket fridges and freezers in Europe.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Artificial intelligence systems are transforming the way software vulnerabilities are discovered.Credit: Hailshadow/Getty.

The disruption of multiple computer systems run by Microsoft, US air traffic control, the bank JPMorgan Chase and even the US National Security Agency has renewed concerns about the resilience of critical digital infrastructure.

At the same time, researchers have reported artificial intelligence -assisted discovery of security flaws in Java and PHP software, while hackers have used AI tools to target supermarket fridges and freezers in Europe.

Sources indicate that although probably unrelated, these incidents highlight a broader transformation in cybersecurity, say researchers. Artificial intelligence is changing how software vulnerabilities are discovered, allowing both attackers and security specialists to examine vast quantities of computer code at unprecedented speed.

Industry observers note that “I think vulnerability discovery without AI is basically dead,” says Steven Murdoch, a computer security researcher at University College London. Researchers in the field who don’t use the technology now risk falling behind, he says.

AI can find weaknesses in software much faster than humans can, giving attackers time to exploit vulnerabilities before organizations can fix them. Researchers now want to understand how thoroughly AI can check software for security flaws, and whether it could introduce new weaknesses.

Agentic systems help attackers identify security vulnerabilities more rapidly and systematically. While hackers previously had to spend hours inspecting websites and probing software for weaknesses that offered unauthorized access to networks, AI agents use automated tools that can search millions of lines of computer code.

Google has reported that attackers have already used agentic AI to examine software updates, identify the security problems they address, and then find ways to exploit them.

NEWS: Cyberattacks are hitting research institutions — with devastating effects.

NEWS: Cyberattacks are hitting research institutions — with devastating effects.

Recent findings suggest that “For me, it's about the scale,” indicates Daniel Gardham, a cybersecurity researcher at the University of Surrey. AI tends to find the same kinds of weaknesses as human hackers, but it makes it easier for people with limited technical expertise to break into systems.

“They can set an AI agent off and come back in 20 minutes and have dozens of results already,” he claims.

Even with AI, most security breaches still involve human failure, he claims, such as weak passwords (a common problem with Europe’s supermarket freezers was that passwords were defaults such as ‘admin’ or ‘12345’) or clicking on links from unfamiliar sources. AI-crafted messages can make such phishing messages more convincing and so more likely to succeed. They can draw on publicly available information to personalize fraudulent communications and make them appear authentic.

Recent findings suggest that murdoch says AI is particularly good at discovering familiar kinds of software flaws, even if the most accomplished human researchers remain better at finding entirely latest types of weakness. “They don't need to sleep,” he says. “You can happily work a hundred of them in parallel.”.

Recent findings suggest that these capabilities of AI helped discover security flaws in Java and PHP software, two programming languages that build cross-platform software and websites. In the Java case, for example, AI identified circumstances that could allow an attacker to corrupt computer memory. But Murdoch claims the significance of the issue has been exaggerated.

The Java vulnerability, he states: “Is a real problem, but it’s not one of the top ten vulnerabilities this year or probably even this week.”.

It has been revealed that just like hackers, cybersecurity researchers are using AI tools to quickly and efficiently find weaknesses in computer systems. Murdoch says this has become increasingly crucial to vulnerability researchers, who can now examine much larger quantities of software and work out how to patch up the defences where necessary. Researchers are also developing AI agents that can detect and repair vulnerabilities automatically.

When security researchers uncover a weakness, they typically notify the software developer privately, allowing engineers to prepare a remedy before publishing details of the problem.

AI is set to completely transform cybersecurity — here’s how researchers must prepare.

AI is set to completely transform cybersecurity — here’s how researchers must prepare.

Murdoch claims the use of AI in cyber security has shortened the time window between public disclosure and attempted exploitation – from several weeks, to just a few days.

According to recent reports, rushing an revision can bring its own problems. A software patch can interfere with other programs and cause the sort of outage that organisations are trying to avoid.

“The life for the defenders who are trying to fix things has become significantly harder,” Murdoch indicates.

It’s unlikely that the recent tech outages were connected as large-scale cyber-attack, notes Murdoch. The most prominent disruptions, he says, are likely technical malfunctions rather than anything more sinister.

Inter Miami star Lionel Messi was lucky not to have been sent off after hurling the ball in the face of his opponent during an embarrassing MLS Cup Playoff defeat.

It has been revealed that in the Round of 16 contest against the Columbus Crew, Miami went down 1-0 early in the first half with a penalty converted by Gonzalo Tapia. The deficit was then compounded when Miami fullback Gonzalo Lujan was sent off with a second yellow card.

On the stroke of halftime, Messi nearly joined his teammate in the locker room with a moment of madness on a throw-in.

Tapia and Messi were both standing out of bounds as the Chilean striker prevented the World Cup winner from taking his throw right away.

Messi then used the ball to shove Tapia's face back. When the Columbus man tried jumping in the air to block the throw, Messi then threw the ball into Tapia's head.

Tapia crumbled to the ground as Messi raised his hands asking for a foul on the Crew star.

Lionel Messi takes a throw-in off Gonzalo Tapia's face pic.twitter.com/jX3tTuojHe.

Lionel Messi nearly got sent off during his team's MLS Cup Playoff match against Columbus.

A frustrated Messi launched the ball off the face of Crew striker Gonzalo Tapia as he prevented the Argentina star from taking a quick throw in. Both players received yellow cards.

Tapia got revenge by scoring a brace to lead the Crew to a 3-0 victory on Saturday evening.

Referee Allen Chapman was not happy with either player's antics, showing yellow cards to both Tapia and Messi.

But ultimately, Columbus and Tapia would get the last laugh as they won 3-0 in the best-of-three Round of 16.

Midfielder Taha Habroune scored the second goal of the evening in the 52nd minute as Tapia secured a brace just six minutes later.

In a recent development, the result has Inter Miami on the brink of elimination from the playoffs after winning the title last season. Columbus dominated every facet of the game, thanks in part to owning 62 percent of possession.

Messi attempted two shots on the evening – counting for half of the saves from Crew keeper Patrick Schulte.

Inter Miami must win the next match in Ohio to stay in the playoffs. If the game finishes tied, the rules dictate the match will proceed directly to penalty kicks.

Industry observers note that out of his three prior seasons in the United States, Messi's 2025 MLS Cup victory was an outlier. Miami missed the playoffs in 2023 and were eliminated in the first round in 2024.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As Nvidia, one of the world's most valuable companies, grapples with CEO Jensen Huang's romantic relationship with an alleged Chinese spy, attention is turning to the much smaller manufacturer she worked for.

Recent findings suggest that alice H., the alleged spy, worked as an executive for Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center and AI computing manufacturer. It manages data center access, including for some major Chinese tech firms such as Alibaba.

According to Megaspeed's website as of November 2026, the tech giant advertises itself as an "Nvidia cloud partner", saying it provides "computing power product services covering Nvidia's entire GPU product line." GPU stands for Graphic Processing Unit, a specialized electronic circuit that are in high demand for artificial intelligence (AI) applications, because they are designed to handle high numbers of parallel mathematical calculations. Megaspeed says it provides access for clients to Nvidia's advanced GB200 NVL72 ​computing system.

This type of firm is often referred to as a "neocloud". It buys Nvidia chips and computing power and then rents it out — in this case, at multiple sites across south-east Asia, to different companies. The US has set up strict export controls to prevent that Nvidia's high-performance chips end up in China, because it sees China as a competitor in the global AI race. It also does not want data centers made up of Nvidia chips to be owned by Chinese companies. It does, however, tolerate that data center compute with Nvidia chips be rented out to Chinese companies like Alibaba, and occasionally allows the export of Nvidia chips for specific purposes.

Megaspeed has bought billions of dollars worth of Nvidia's products in recent years and has been accused of breaching US export controls to divert Nvidia chips into China.

In December 2025, Bloomberg reported that the "once-obscure" Megaspeed had become the biggest buyer of Nvidia's chips in all of south-east Asia and that the US government was investigating its ownership structure and whether or not it was smuggling Nvidia chips into China.

At the same time, Singapore police began an investigation into whether or not Megaspeed had "violated local laws" without specifying which ones. Those investigations are believed to be still ongoing.

On December 23, 2025, Megaspeed strenuously denied any wrongdoing in a statement — which still appears as the first page for visitors to the manufacturer's website as of November 2026.

According to recent reports, "There has been no evidence of any violations concerning the illicit transfer of chips or any illegal activities, and this demonstrates that we are a compliant and legitimate company," it remarked. "We operate fully within the bounds of all applicable export control regulations and maintain the highest standards of legal and ethical conduct.".

According to recent reports, the US government investigation began in 2024. The Commerce Department initially began looking into Megaspeed, but the US Justice Department has since taken over. According to the Fresh York Times, this switch came about after an Nvidia executive directly contacted the Commerce Department about the investigation.

Megaspeed was founded in 2015 and was originally called 7Road International. It changed its name to Megaspeed in March 2023. It is owned by the Singapore-registered Swiftdata, which was set up in October 2023.

Its rise in prominence coincided with a sharp increase in assets, which increased from $33 million in 2023 to $3 billion in 2024.

Alice H., the woman accused of being a Chinese spy, had an affair with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. She is widely seen as an influential figurehead at Megaspeed. She also served as the manufacturer's managing director of Megaspeed for eight months in 2023.

Sources indicate that the Financial Times reported on Monday that Alice H. leveraged her close access to Jensen Huang and Nvidia to pitch AI chips deals to Chinese investors.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

It has been revealed that the newspaper remarked that in early 2025, Alice H. sought investment in China for a data center project in south-east Asia, and cited their easy access to Nvidia chips and close relationship with Alibaba.

Alibaba lent money to Megaspeed in June 2024, via subsidiaries. It has remained Megaspeed's largest client, according to reporting by the Financial Times.

It has been revealed that in December 2025, Nvidia mentioned its own inquiry into Megaspeed had found no evidence of chips being diverted and that the tech giant was fully owned and operated outside of China, with no Chinese shareholders. The company told Bloomberg at the time that it had visited Megaspeed's facilities on multiple occasions and had seen nothing untoward.

Megaspeed is one of several companies accused of smuggling Nvidia's chips into China or finding ways to give Chinese companies access to them.

Nvidia's high-performance chips are seen as essential for companies looking for the most advanced form of supercomputing to use and develop various AI applications.

Back in 2022, the Biden Administration began severely restricting the sale of the US's most advanced chips to China, part of the two countries' growing rivalry to achieve AI dominance.

However, an illegal smuggling and underground network was soon set up, with many vendors operating to get the chips into China and selling them on to companies there.

In December 2025, US authorities shut down the operations of Hao Global, a US-based shell company with links to China which plead guilty to smuggling Nvidia chips to China.

In June 2026, Taiwanese government agencies raided the offices of Super Micro Computer as part of an investigation into the smuggling of Nvidia chips to China.

While export restrictions have been eased significantly under the Trump administration, there are still significant blocks and restrictions on the most advanced Nvidia chips.

In December 2025, the Trump administration approved several Chinese companies to buy or handle advanced Nvidia H200 chips, a move that sparked significant concern among the US security establishment.

However, that deal has not led to a significant flow of Nvidia chips moving legally to China, amid strict US licencing controls and official reluctance from Beijing to publicly promote Nvidia chips to the detriment of its own alternatives.

This was the afternoon when Xabi Alonso’s Chelsea went from swashbuckling to stoic, thrilling to tenacious.

For all Alonso’s attacking vigour at the start of his reign, there can have been no more symbolically satisfying victory under the new coach than this resolute win at Everton – the most vivid example of an increasingly impressive transformation.

Where recently they wilted, on Saturday they thrived in securing a first Premier League clean sheet for nine months.

Much more of this and the adjectives which were splattered across Chelsea during the golden years of José Mourinho – solid, robust and dogged – will be part of the Stamford Bridge lexicon once more.

According to recent reports, “Just one day,” Alonso warned, both acclaiming the importance of the win while wisely preaching caution. “It will be key when we manage 10 clean sheets, even though this one feels good. We need to repeat it again and again, but the mentality was very good. Sometimes it is not to play nice, it is to play good – to win second balls, and to be efficient. “What we know is that he left the stadium conscious and is now in hospital undergoing precautionary tests.

Industry observers note that “We need to wait. Hopefully it will not be too serious, but at the moment we just have to wait.”.

Alonso is speedily shifting perceptions of this previously underperforming bunch, the Stamford Bridge culture on and off the pitch already unrecognisable from a few months ago.

Chelsea captain Reece James’ surgery could be out for a couple of months, Xabi Alonso explained.

Sources indicate that he told the  press: “I wish him the best recovery. We won’t set timelines, but we expect him to be out for several weeks. It’s not going to be short. Whether it’s before or after Christmas then time will tell. It needs to be done properly.”.

Recent findings suggest that he is looking to vice captains Moises Caceido and Levi Colwill to step up in his absence, explaining: “You can be a captain without an armband, for sure. Leadership is important and that’s why we have this group, not just on matchday.”.

James remains vital to Chelsea at their best, and while his minutes have been managed, it’s a huge disappointment to see him need to go under the knife once more.

In a recent development, in his press conference ahead of the weekend, Everton boss David Moyes was not too concerned by his relatively small squad.He said:  “Leicester City won the league with not too many players. We have not got too many players. I am not saying we’re going to win the league, but we want to try to challenge and be around the top teams.”.

In a recent development, that might be made harder by the news that the Friedkin Group are already looking to sell the club after only a couple of years in charge. Moyes is a rare thing, a manager who keeps improving despite setbacks, and his second spell has been fairly solid so far.

Moyes is aware that Chelsea pose a threat up front, adding: “Their attacking line is incredibly exciting. I also think they have got some super defenders as well, but they are playing quite an expansive game, which on its day can lead to goals and on another day it can lead to defeats.”.

Welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of Everton vs Chelsea.

Chelsea return to Premier League action this weekend looking to harness the momentum of their emphatic 5-1 victory over Bournemouth before the international break. That Stamford Bridge masterclass ended a frustrating three-match winless streak and was built upon braces from Joao Pedro and Jordan Henderson, alongside another strike from summer signing Morgan Rogers.

Yet the true catalyst for the resurgence was the return of Moises Caicedo. Having shaken off the calf problem that hindered his early-season involvement, the midfielder anchored the side’s win. While defensive vulnerabilities persist - extending an unwanted run of league matches without a clean sheet back to January - the victory offered clear signs of progress under their head coach, Xabi Alonso.

Sources indicate that next up is a notoriously difficult trip to Merseyside to face Everton in Saturday’s lunchtime fixture. Historically, Everton have proven to be a formidable stumbling block for the capital club, particularly on home turf. Everton enter the weekend unbeaten in eight of their last nine home encounters against Chelsea, a stretch that has seen the Londoners fail to score on seven visits and suffer six defeats, including a chastening 3-0 reverse last term that spelt the end for Liam Rosenior.

David Moyes will demand a sharper defensive showing from his side this time around, following a frustrating 2-2 draw with Hull City where a 2-1 lead slipped away. Even so, Everton’s broader defensive record at home offers encouragement, having kept clean sheets in two of their opening three league fixtures at their base.

With both teams eager to build consistency, Saturday’s clash pits Chelsea’s newly found attacking spark against an opponent that traditionally relishes this fixture.
